readerTitle: Raise the bus fare? First ask who can walk away
caseNote: 가상 사례 (시내버스, 화물 운송사, 협업 소프트웨어) + 대중교통 요금 탄력성에 관한 실제 연구 경향 · 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격 인상의 결과는 평균 고객이 아니라 '대안이 있는 고객'과 '시간이 지난 뒤의 고객'이 정한다.
misconception: 요금을 올린 첫 달에 고객이 거의 줄지 않았다면 가격 인상은 성공한 것이다.

sources.text: Litman, T. Transit Price Elasticities and Cross-Elasticities. Victoria Transport Policy Institute (단기 탄력성은 낮고 장기 탄력성은 더 높다는 연구 정리)
버스, 화물 운송사, 소프트웨어 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "대중교통 이용은 단기에는 요금 변화에 덜 민감하고, 몇 년에 걸쳐 더 민감해진다"는 서술은 Litman(VTPI) 정리에 근거합니다. 카드에는 구체적 탄력성 수치를 연구 결과로 제시하지 않고 가정값(0.3, 0.6)으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문을 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Raise the bus fare? First ask who can walk away
body: A city bus service is short of money. The board proposes raising the fare from $2.00 to $2.40.
At the stop, one rider shrugs: she has no car. Another frowns: he could drive, or cycle when it's sunny. The same 40 cents means two very different things to them.

image.label: Two riders at a bus stop reacting to a new fare sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 버스 정류장에 "$2.00 → $2.40" 안내판. 한 사람은 담담하게 버스를 기다리고, 다른 한 사람은 옆의 자전거와 자동차 열쇠를 바라봄. 실제 교통 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: What happens after a 20% fare rise?
body: The service carries 100,000 rides a day at $2.00. The fare goes up 20%. What's most likely in the first few months?

options.text: Fare revenue falls, because riders flee
options.feedback: That happens when demand is very price-sensitive. For many riders the bus is a necessity with no easy substitute, so *price elasticity* is low in the short run.

options.text: Riders drop a little, and fare revenue rises
options.feedback: Right for the short run. Low price elasticity means ridership falls by less than the fare rises. The catch comes later.
Close for riders with no other option. But some riders do have choices, and they react first.

cards.title: Short run vs a few years later.
body: Assumed responses: riders fall 6% at first, then 12% as people adjust. Revenue still rises, but the gain shrinks by more than half.

cards.title: Necessity for some, choice for others.
body: **Price elasticity** measures how much demand moves when price moves. It isn't one number for the whole city.
For riders without a car, the bus is a **necessity**: they keep riding and pay more. For riders with a car, a bike or a flexible schedule, it's closer to a choice. They are the ones who leave.
So the real question isn't "will riders leave?" It's "which riders, and how many of them have options?"

image.label: Riders split into those with alternatives and those without
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 그룹 "No alternative"는 버스에 그대로 탑승, 오른쪽 그룹 "Has alternatives"는 자동차, 자전거, 재택근무 아이콘으로 흩어짐. 오른쪽 화살표가 더 굵음.

cards.title: Elasticity grows with time.
body: Transport research has long found that riders respond less to fares in the short run than over several years.

Next month, people still ride. Next year, some buy a car, move closer to work or join a carpool. Each of those choices is hard to reverse. The first months make a price rise look cheaper than it really is.

cards.title: Higher revenue can hide a weaker business.
body: A bus costs about the same to run with 40 riders or 30. Losing riders saves little, so lost rides hurt more than the revenue table shows.
If revenue gains lead to service cuts, more riders with options leave. That can become a spiral.
And the riders who stay are often the ones who can least afford it. Customers may judge that as unfair, and that hurts trust too.

cards.title: Now it's a freight company.
body: You deliver spare parts by truck. Some customers are factories with a broken machine waiting. Others are retailers shipping routine stock, who compare carriers every quarter.
Costs are up. How do you raise prices?

options.feedback: Simple and easy to explain. But the routine shippers are the price-sensitive ones, and they may move their volume to a rival.

options.text: Raise urgent delivery rates more, keep routine rates close to today
options.feedback: Urgent parts are a necessity with few substitutes, so that demand has low elasticity. You protect the volume most likely to leave.

options.text: Raise routine rates most, since that's where the volume is
options.feedback: More volume means more money per percent, but also the customers with the most options. High elasticity can turn a rate rise into a revenue drop.

cards.title: Now it's a team software tool.
body: You raised your price from $10 to $12 per seat. In the first month, almost no customers cancel. Most pay yearly. Your team wants to call it a success.

options.text: Agree. Low cancellations prove demand is not price-sensitive
options.feedback: Yearly customers can't react until renewal. Short-run elasticity looks low partly because leaving takes time.

options.text: Track renewals and seat counts over the next 12 months
options.feedback: That shows the long-run elasticity. Some teams cut seats instead of leaving, which a cancellation count misses.

options.text: Ask customers in a survey if the price is fair
options.feedback: Useful for spotting anger early. But what people say and what they do at renewal can differ.

cards.title: Price for the customers who can leave, and wait to judge.
body: Used here: **price elasticity**, which grows over time, and **necessities vs luxuries**, which decide who stays and who leaves.
**Try it today:** split your customers into two groups: those with an easy alternative and those without. Which group would a price rise really test?
